titleText.es: Y el diario está lleno con todas las cosas que le diría a ella si yo fuera agradable como tú. Lo quemo cuando está lleno.
titleText.en: And the journal is filled with all the things I'd say to her if I were nice like you. I burn it when it's full.
titleText.noteEn: The title text sharpens the joke: Black Hat writes down the kind things he withholds from the woman, then burns the journal.

applications.explanationEn: Llevas is the form of llevar for one familiar person, and un diario supplies the record being kept.

regions.labelEs: AH, EN EL TREN FINJO QUE ESCRIBO EN ÉL Y ESPERO A QUE UNA CHICA TÍMIDA SE SIENTE ENFRENTE.

applications.exampleEs: ESPERO A QUE UNA CHICA TÍMIDA SE SIENTE
applications.explanationEn: Espero a que presents an awaited event; una chica tímida names who will perform it, and se siente is the special form of sentarse used because the sitting is not yet a fact.

regions.labelEs: MIRO HACIA ELLA Y ESPERO A QUE HAYA CONTACTO VISUAL, LUEGO BAJO LA MIRADA CON TIMIDEZ Y, SI PUEDO, ME SONROJO.

applications.exampleEs: ESPERO A QUE HAYA CONTACTO VISUAL
applications.explanationEn: Espero a que sets up an awaited event, haya is the special existential form used because it is not yet a fact, and contacto visual names what the speaker is waiting to exist.
Contacto and visual form the conventional two-word expression taught by this card.
Bajo is the first-person form of bajar, while la mirada names the gaze being lowered.

regions.labelEs: LUEGO, CUANDO VEO QUE ELLA EMPIEZA A SONREÍRME, PONGO LOS OJOS EN BLANCO Y LE LANZO UNA MIRADA RÁPIDA, Y RETOMO LA ESCRITURA.

applications.explanationEn: Empieza marks the beginning, a links it to the action, and sonreír remains in its unchanged dictionary form with me attached.
Me is attached directly to the unchanged verb sonreír, and the written accent on í remains.
Pongo is the first-person form of poner, followed by the fixed words los ojos en blanco.
Le marks the person receiving the look, lanzo is the first-person form of lanzar, and una mirada names the look.

regions.labelEs: LA ALIENACIÓN SE LE QUEDA PARA TODO EL DÍA. ES GENIAL.

applications.explanationEn: Para introduces the stated span here. With quedarse and a simple elapsed duration, many speakers would more naturally use durante todo el día.
Todo matches the masculine time word día, and Spanish keeps the article el between them.

regions.labelEs: ERES REPUGNANTE. POR ESTAS COSAS NO PODEMOS SALIR CON GENTE AGRADABLE.
NO PUEDO EVITARLO. ES COMO QUITARLE UN CARAMELO A UN NIÑO SOLITARIO Y DEPRESIVO.

applications.explanationEn: No negates puedo, and evitarlo keeps evitar in its unchanged dictionary form with lo attached.
Lo is attached directly to the unchanged verb evitar and identifies the thing that cannot be avoided.
Le is attached directly to the unchanged verb quitar and identifies the person affected by the removal.

applications.exampleEs: QUITARLE UN CARAMELO A UN NIÑO
applications.explanationEn: Quitar has le attached for the affected person, un caramelo fills the thing slot, and a un niño makes that person explicit.

cards.noteEn: Desde marks the point when a period begins. Before a question word such as cuándo, it asks for that starting point.

example.en: I have worked here since January.

cards.noteEn: Cuándo has an accent when it asks, directly or indirectly, at what time something happens.
Llevar often means ‘to carry’ or ‘to wear,’ but with a journal, record, or account it can mean to keep or maintain it.

example.en: You keep a very clear record.

cards.questionEn: How do you say that someone keeps a journal or diary?
cards.answerEn: Use a form of llevar with diario.
cards.noteEn: Llevar changes to show who keeps the journal and when. In this collocation it means ‘to keep’ or ‘maintain,’ not to carry the journal physically.

example.es: Marta lleva un diario de viaje.

cards.noteEn: Ah can show that the speaker has just understood, noticed, or recognized something. Its exact English equivalent depends on tone.
Finjo is the present ‘I’ form of fingir, ‘to pretend.’ Its g changes to j before the ending -o.
Que introduces a clause after verbs such as creer, saber, esperar, or decir. English often uses “that,” but may leave it unstated.

example.en: I think that Ana is coming.

cards.answerEn: it (referring back to a masculine singular thing)
cards.noteEn: Él normally means “he” or “him,” but after a preposition it can also replace a masculine singular thing already named. English then uses “it.” Keep the accent to distinguish él from el, “the.”

example.es: El ruido es fuerte, pero me acostumbré a él.
example.en: The noise is loud, but I got used to it.

cards.noteEn: Esperar can mean either “to wait” or “to hope/expect.” When no hoped-for event or object follows, context can give it the simple meaning “to wait.”

cards.questionEn: How do you say that someone waits for another person or event to do something?
cards.answerEn: Use a form of esperar, then a que, then put the awaited action in the subjunctive form.
cards.noteEn: The subjunctive is a special verb form used here because the awaited event has not happened yet. Esperar changes for the person and time; a que stays fixed. The awaited verb changes too: ordinary llega becomes llegue in espero a que llegue. If the waiting person will perform the later action, Spanish instead uses esperar a followed by the action verb's unchanged dictionary form.

example.en: I am waiting for Marta to arrive.

cards.answerEn: no separate English word; required in esperar a que
cards.noteEn: When esperar means waiting for an event, Spanish uses a between esperar and que. Keep all three pieces together: esperar a que.

example.es: Espero a que termine la lluvia.
example.en: I am waiting for the rain to end.

cards.answerEn: no separate English word; completes esperar a que before an awaited event
cards.noteEn: Que introduces the event being awaited after esperar a. English usually folds this link into ‘wait for’ rather than translating que separately.

example.es: Esperamos a que llegue el autobús.
example.en: We are waiting for the bus to arrive.

cards.answerEn: no separate English word; marks sentarse, ‘to sit down’
cards.noteEn: Sentarse uses a matching short word: me, te, se, nos, or os. Use se with él, ella, usted, ellos, ellas, or ustedes.

example.es: Ella se sienta junto a la ventana.
example.en: She sits down by the window.

cards.noteEn: Se siente here comes from sentarse, ‘to sit down,’ not sentirse, ‘to feel.’ After wording that presents the sitting as still awaited, ordinary se sienta changes to the special form se siente.

example.es: Espero a que Luis se siente.
example.en: I am waiting for Luis to sit down.

cards.noteEn: Enfrente can describe the position directly opposite. Enfrente de adds the person or thing that serves as the reference point.
After a preposition such as con, ella corresponds to her. As a sentence subject, it means she.

cards.answerEn: there is; there is to be (subjunctive form)
cards.noteEn: Haya is the special form related to hay, ‘there is’ or ‘there are.’ It appears when the existence of something is awaited, wanted, doubted, or otherwise not presented as an established fact.

example.en: I am waiting for there to be space.

cards.questionEn: How do you say ‘eye contact’ in Spanish?
cards.noteEn: Spanish names this kind of contact with visual, ‘related to sight.’ It does not use the word ojo, ‘eye,’ in this expression.
Bajo is the present ‘I’ form of bajar here. The same written form can also mean ‘low’ or ‘under’ in other contexts.

cards.questionEn: How do you say that someone lowers their gaze or looks down?
cards.answerEn: Use a form of bajar followed by la mirada.
cards.noteEn: Bajar changes for the person and time. La mirada stays as the thing being lowered and refers to the person's gaze rather than a physical object.
Mirada can name the act or manner of looking, and it can also mean a way of viewing a topic.

example.es: El libro ofrece una mirada distinta al problema.
example.en: The book offers a different look at the problem.

cards.answerEn: no separate English word here; marks an “I” verb that is used with me
cards.noteEn: Some Spanish verbs conventionally come with me, te, se, nos, or os even when no one literally acts on themselves. Me marks the speaker's form. English usually absorbs it into the verb's meaning.
Sonrojo is the present ‘I’ form of sonrojarse, ‘to blush.’ In this use it appears with me: me sonrojo.

cards.questionEn: How do you say that someone starts doing an action?
cards.answerEn: Use a form of empezar, then a, then the action verb in its unchanged dictionary form.
cards.noteEn: The plus sign means “followed by.” The dictionary form, also called the infinitive, is the unchanged form ending in -ar, -er, or -ir. Empezar changes for the person and time; a stays fixed, and the action verb stays unchanged.

cards.answerEn: to (linking a verb to the following infinitive)

cards.noteEn: Sonreír means ‘to smile.’ The short word me is attached to its end and identifies the person receiving the smile; the written accent on í remains.

example.en: She wants to smile at me.

cards.promptEs: verbo en forma de diccionario + pronombre unido
cards.questionEn: Where can a short object word such as me, te, lo, or la go with an unchanged action verb?
cards.answerEn: Attach it to the end of the verb and write the result as one word.
cards.noteEn: An unchanged dictionary-form verb ends in -ar, -er, or -ir. Short object words can attach directly: conocer + te becomes conocerte, and ayudar + me becomes ayudarme.

cards.answerEn: I roll (my eyes; in poner los ojos en blanco)
cards.noteEn: Pongo is the present ‘I’ form of poner, normally ‘to put.’ In the complete expression poner los ojos en blanco, natural English uses ‘to roll one's eyes.’

example.es: Pongo los ojos en blanco sin querer.

cards.questionEn: How do you say that someone rolls their eyes?
cards.answerEn: Use a form of poner followed by los ojos en blanco.
cards.noteEn: Only poner changes for the person and time; los ojos en blanco stays fixed. The expression describes the familiar gesture of showing annoyance, disbelief, or impatience and is not translated word by word.

example.es: Clara puso los ojos en blanco.

cards.answerEn: no separate English word; part of poner los ojos en blanco
cards.noteEn: En links ojos to blanco inside the fixed expression for rolling one's eyes. Translate the complete expression rather than this en on its own.

example.es: No pongas los ojos en blanco.

cards.answerEn: no separate English word; completes the expression for rolling one's eyes
cards.noteEn: Blanco ordinarily means ‘white.’ In poner los ojos en blanco, it is a fixed part of the expression rather than a separate color description in natural English.

example.es: Él puso los ojos en blanco.

cards.answerEn: her; to her (marks the female recipient)
cards.noteEn: Le identifies the person who receives a request or another action. The same Spanish form can also mean “to him” or formal “to you”; context identifies the person.

cards.questionEn: How do you say that someone gives another person a look?
cards.answerEn: Use a form of lanzar and una mirada, with a short person word such as le to mark who receives the look.
cards.noteEn: Lanzar changes for the person and time. The short word identifies who receives the look: me for me, te for you, le for him or her, nos for us, os for you all in Spain, and les for them. A named recipient can follow a, as in le lanza una mirada a Luis.

example.es: Marta le lanza una mirada a Luis.

cards.noteEn: Lanzar usually means ‘to throw.’ With mirada, it forms the conventional expression for casting or giving someone a look.

example.en: I cast a glance at the clock.

cards.answerEn: no separate English word; marks quedarse, “to remain” or “stay”
cards.noteEn: Quedar and quedarse have several uses. With se here, the subject continues to be present rather than leaving.

cards.answerEn: her; marks the person affected by a situation or result
cards.noteEn: Le can identify one person affected by what happens even when natural English does not use ‘to.’ A phrase beginning with a can make that person explicit: se le queda a Ana.

example.es: A Laura se le quedó esa sensación.

cards.noteEn: Para can introduce a period assigned to or covered by something, such as a reservation or pass. When simply describing how long an action continues, durante is often more natural.

example.es: La reserva es para toda la tarde.
example.en: The reservation is for the whole afternoon.

cards.questionEn: How do you say that something lasts for an entire day, night, or other time period?
cards.answerEn: Put todo or toda before the usual word for ‘the’ and the time period: todo el día, toda la noche.
cards.noteEn: Todo changes to match the time word: use todo with a masculine word such as día and toda with a feminine word such as noche. Spanish keeps el or la in this pattern even though natural English normally omits ‘the’ and says ‘all day’ or ‘all night.’

cards.answerEn: to go out (socially or for entertainment)
cards.noteEn: Salir can mean simply leaving a place, but it also commonly means going out to socialize, eat, drink, dance, or enjoy entertainment.

cards.promptEs: no poder evitar + nombre o verbo en forma de diccionario
cards.questionEn: How do you say that someone cannot help doing an action or cannot avoid a feeling?
cards.answerEn: Use no, a form of poder, evitar, and then the action or feeling that cannot be avoided.
cards.noteEn: Only poder changes for the person and time; evitar remains in its unchanged dictionary form. Another action also stays in its dictionary form: no puedo evitar reír means “I cannot help laughing.” A noun can follow instead, as in no pudo evitar la duda.

cards.answerEn: to help it; to avoid it
cards.noteEn: Evitar means ‘to avoid,’ and lo, ‘it,’ is attached to the end. In no puedo evitarlo, natural English commonly says ‘I can't help it.’
Unaccented como can introduce the person, thing, or situation used for a comparison. It does not ask “how”; the question word cómo has an accent.

cards.answerEn: to take away from him or her
cards.noteEn: Quitar means ‘to take away’ or ‘remove.’ The attached le identifies the person deprived of something; the thing being taken normally follows.

example.en: I want to take the toy away from him.

cards.promptEs: me/te/le/nos/os/les + quitar + cosa (+ a alguien o algo)
cards.questionEn: How do you say that someone takes one thing away from another person or thing?
cards.answerEn: Use a short word such as me or le with quitar, then name the thing taken away. You can add a followed by the person or thing that is deprived of it.
cards.noteEn: Quitar changes for the person and time. The short word identifies the person or thing that loses something: me, te, le, nos, os, or les. With an unchanged dictionary-form verb, attach it as in quitarle; with a changed verb, place it before, as in le quita or me quitaste. Spanish can repeat or clarify the affected entity after a, even though English uses ‘from’ or a possessive. In the prompt, each plus sign means ‘followed by,’ and the parentheses mark the optional clarifying phrase.

example.es: Ana le quita el juguete a Luis.
example.en: Ana takes the toy away from Luis.

cards.answerEn: from; introduces the person or thing something is taken from
cards.noteEn: After quitarle, a can introduce or clarify the person or thing that loses something. Natural English uses ‘from’ even though Spanish uses a.

example.es: Le quitan el balón a Pablo.
example.en: They take the ball away from Pablo.

cards.noteEn: Depresivo can describe a depressive tendency or a gloomy quality. Deprimido is more usual for saying that someone feels depressed at a particular moment.

example.es: La novela tiene un tono depresivo.
example.en: The novel has a gloomy tone.
